content.title: About
content.content: Romaine lettuce (Lactuca sativa var. longifolia) is a leaf lettuce variety with long, crisp, slightly bitter leaves. Grown in temperate climates, it is usually eaten raw in salads, sandwiches, and wraps.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Romaine gets its name from the ancient Roman city of Rome, where it was cultivated as early as the 1st century AD.
Its leaves contain more vitamin K than most other lettuce types.
Romaine is the classic base for Caesar salad because of its sturdy texture.
Unlike tender leaf lettuces, romaine stays fresh longer—up to a week in the refrigerator.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene in the leaves converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immunity.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Romaine leaves provide polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Leaf vegetable allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lettuce.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw lettuce can harbor salmonella or E. coli if not handled hygienically.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic produce, rinse the leaves thoroughly to reduce pesticide exposure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Romaine is typically eaten raw: in salads, sandwiches, wraps, or as a crunchy side to meat dishes. Toss the leaves with a splash of lemon juice or vinegar to mellow the slight bitterness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store romaine in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or a container with a damp paper towel. Properly stored, it stays fresh for 7–10 days.
